## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.91135.3.sa2](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.91135.3.sa2)

Summary:

We often have prior expectations about how the sensory world will change, but it remains an open question as to how these expectations are integrated into perceptual decisions. In particular, scientists have debated whether prior knowledge principally changes the decisions we make about the perceptual world, or directly alters our perceptual encoding of incoming sensory evidence.

The authors aimed to shed light on this conundrum by using a novel psychophysical task while measuring EEG signals that have previously been linked to either the sensory encoding or response selection phase of perceptual choice. The results convincingly demonstrate that both features of perceptual decision making are modulated by prior expectations - but that these biases in neural process emerge over different time courses (i.e., decisional signals are shaped early in learning, but biases in sensory processing are slower to emerge).

Another interesting observation unearthed in the study - though not strictly linked to this perceptual/decisional puzzle - is that neural signatures of focused attention are exaggerated on trials where participants are given neutral (i.e. uninformative) cues. This is consistent with the idea that observers are more attentive to incoming sensory evidence when they cannot rely on their expectations.

In general, I think the study makes a strong contribution to the literature, and does an excellent job of separating 'perceiving' from 'responding'. More perhaps could have been done though to separate 'perceiving' and 'responding' from 'deciding' (see below).

Strengths:

The work is executed expertly and focuses cleverly on two features of the EEG signals that can be closely connected to specific loci of the perceptual decision making process - the SSVEP which connects closely to sensory (visual) encoding, and Mu-Beta lateralisation which connects closely to movement preparation. This is a very appropriate design choice given the authors' research question.

Another advantage of the design is the use of an unusually long training regime (i.e., for humans) - which makes it possible to probe the emergence of different expectation biases in the brain over different timecourses, and in a way that may be more comparable to work with nonhuman animals (who are routinely trained for much longer than humans).

Weaknesses:

In my view, the principal shortcoming of this study is that the experimental task confounds expectations about stimulus identity with expectations about to-be-performed responses. That is, cues in the task don't just tell participants what they will (probably) see, but what they (probably) should do.

In many respects, this feature of the paradigm might seem inevitable, as if specific stimuli are not connected to specific responses, it is not possible to observe motor preparation of this kind (e.g., de Lange, Rahnev, Donner & Lau, 2013 - JoN).

However, the theoretical models that the authors focus on (e.g., drift diffusion models) are models of decision (i.e., commitment to a proposition about the world) as much as they are models of choice (i.e., commitment to action). Expectation researchers interested in these models are often interested in asking whether predictions influence perceptual processing, perceptual decision and/or response selection stages (e.g., Feuerriegel, Blom & Hoogendorn, 2021 - Cortex), and other researchers have shown that parameters like drift bias and start point bias can be shifted in paradigms where observers cannot possibly prepare a response (e.g., Thomas, Yon, de Lange & Press, 2020 - Psych Sci).

The present paradigm used by Walsh et al makes it possible to disentangle sensory processing from later decisional processes, but it blurs together the processes of deciding about the stimulus and choosing/initiating the response. This ultimately limits the insights we can draw from this study - as it remains unclear whether rapid changes in motor preparation we see reflect rapid acquisition of new decision criterion or simple cue-action learning. I think this would be important for comprehensively testing the models the authors target - and a good avenue for future work.

In revising the manuscript after an initial round of revisions, the authors have done a good job of acknowledging these complexities - and I don't think that any of these outstanding scientific puzzles detract from the value of the paper as a whole.

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.91135.3.sa3](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.91135.3.sa3)

Observers make judgements about expected stimuli faster and more accurately. How expectations facilitate such perceptual decisions remains an ongoing area of investigation, however, as expectations may exert their effects in multiple ways. Expectations may directly influence the encoding of sensory signals. Alternatively (or additionally), expectations may influence later stages of decision-making, such as motor preparation, when they bear on the appropriate behavioral response.

In the present study, Walsh and colleagues directly measured the effect of expectations on sensory and motor signals by making clever use of the encephalogram (EEG) recorded from human observers performing a contrast discrimination task. On each trial, a predictive cue indicated which of two superimposed stimuli would likely be higher contrast and, therefore, whether a left or right button press was likely to yield a correct response. Deft design choices allowed the authors to extract both contrast-dependent sensory signals and motor preparation signals from the EEG. The authors provide compelling evidence that, when predictive cues provide information about both a forthcoming stimulus and the appropriate behavioral response, expectation effects are immediately manifest in motor preparation signals and only emerge in sensory signals after extensive training.

Future work should attempt to reconcile these results with related investigations in the field. As the authors note, several groups have reported expectation-induced modulation of sensory signals (using both fMRI and EEG/MEG) on shorter timescales (e.g. just one or two sessions of a few hundred trials, versus the intensive multi-session study reported here). One interesting possibility is that perceptual expectations are not automatic but demand the deployment of feature-based attention, while motor preparation is comparatively less effortful and so dominates when both sources of information are available, as in the present study. This hypothesis is consistent with the authors' thoughtful analysis showing decreased neural signatures of attention over posterior electrodes following predictive cues. Therefore, observing the timescale of sensory effects using the same design and methods (facilitating direct comparison with the present work), but altering task demands slightly such that cues are no longer predictive of the appropriate behavioral response, could be illuminating.

results.result: Predictive cues produced robust behavioral biases in both reaction time and accuracy. Valid cues led to faster correct responses and higher accuracy compared to neutral cues, while invalid cues produced slower correct responses and lower accuracy. These effects remained stable across task exposure.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C40 provide comprehensive statistical evidence (all p<0.001) demonstrating significant main effects of cue validity on both RT and accuracy, with appropriate pairwise comparisons. The lack of interaction with task exposure (C28, C33, C38) is also well-documented. The statistical approach using mixed effects models is appropriate for the repeated-measures design.

results.result: The SSVEP reliably tracked differential contrast evidence, with target gratings producing significantly larger responses than non-target gratings (BF10=500). Marginal SSVEP amplitude significantly predicted both choice accuracy (β=0.009, p=0.023) and reaction time (β=−0.001, p=0.007), validating it as a neural index of sensory evidence encoding.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C47, C73-C74 provide strong convergent evidence that SSVEP tracks contrast and predicts behavior. The Bayesian analysis (C43) provides very strong evidence (BF10=500), and the mixed effects models show significant relationships with both accuracy and RT. This establishes SSVEP as a valid measure of evidence encoding, which is critical for interpreting subsequent findings.

results.result: Predictive cues significantly modulated the marginal SSVEP during evidence presentation (F(2,44553)=4.21, p=0.015). Invalid cues produced significantly reduced SSVEP amplitude compared to both valid (p=0.004) and neutral cues (p=0.037), while valid and neutral conditions did not differ significantly. No anticipatory modulation was observed during the baseline period.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C54, C75 demonstrate a clear pattern: cues modulate sensory encoding during evidence presentation but not in anticipation. The statistical evidence is solid with appropriate mixed effects models and pairwise comparisons. The lack of anticipatory effects (C48) and the specific pattern of invalid cue suppression (C50-C52) are well-documented. The absence of a cue×target interaction (C54, p=0.054) is marginally non-significant but appropriately reported.

results.result: Motor preparation biases (MB lateralization) were present from the earliest trials and remained stable across task exposure, while sensory-level SSVEP modulations only emerged with extended task exposure (~4 hours). A significant interaction between cue validity and task exposure (F(2,44550)=4.31, p=0.013) showed that the invalid cue effect on SSVEP strengthened over time.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C6-C7, C55-C61, C94 provide strong evidence for differential temporal dynamics. The MB analysis (C55-C57) shows significant lateralization with no task exposure effects, while SSVEP analysis (C58-C61) demonstrates a significant interaction. The statistical evidence is robust with appropriate mixed effects models. This temporal dissociation is a key finding supporting the conclusion that sensory modulation emerges gradually rather than being present from the start.

results.result: Analysis of pre- versus post-response SSVEP differences showed no main effect of cue validity (F(2,42605)=2.103, p=0.122) and no interaction with task exposure. Bayesian analysis provided no compelling evidence that cue effects increased post-response (BF10=1.58 for invalid vs neutral; BF10=0.32 for invalid vs valid).
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C66 address whether the observed SSVEP modulation reflects post-decisional confirmation bias. The null results are appropriately supported by both frequentist (non-significant main effects and interactions) and Bayesian analyses (inconclusive Bayes factors). This strengthens the interpretation that cue effects on SSVEP occur during evidence accumulation rather than after choice commitment.

results.result: Pre-evidence alpha-band activity showed significantly greater desynchronization in the neutral cue condition compared to cued conditions (F(1,52527)=10.10, p=0.001), suggesting enhanced stimulus engagement when no predictive information was available. This pattern is consistent with established links between alpha desynchronization and attentional engagement.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C70, C87-C90 provide a coherent account of differential engagement across cue conditions. The statistical evidence (C70) is strong, and the interpretation is well-grounded in established literature about alpha oscillations and attention (C67-C69, C88-C89). This finding helps explain why valid cues did not boost SSVEP relative to neutral cues—participants may have compensated with increased attention in the neutral condition.

results.result: Task difficulty titration resulted in a significant reduction in marginal contrast across task exposure (F(1,58)=7.17, p=0.01), yet participant scores remained stable (F(1,58)=0.004, p=0.953). This suggests participants maintained performance despite reduced physical evidence.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C42, C95 document an important aspect of the experimental design and its consequences. The statistical evidence shows both the reduction in contrast and stability of performance. This pattern is relevant for interpreting the emergence of sensory modulation—participants may have incorporated subtle sensory biases to maintain performance as task difficulty increased.

results.result: The study included 12 participants (11 for SSVEP analyses) who completed an average of 5750 trials across 4-6 sessions. A post-hoc analysis revealed participants were 1.7 times more likely to choose the 20 Hz grating, though this bias was balanced across conditions and could not have influenced the reported effects. The 25 Hz SSVEP had consistently greater amplitude than the 20 Hz signal.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C111, C116-C120 provide transparent reporting of sample characteristics and methodological issues. The frequency bias (C116) is acknowledged as an error in calibration procedures, but the authors provide logical arguments (C118-C119) for why this could not have confounded the main findings due to counterbalancing. The differential SSVEP amplitude by frequency (C120) is appropriately controlled for in statistical models. This transparency is commendable, though the small sample size (n=11-12) limits generalizability.

results.result: The study concludes that probabilistic information can induce subtle biases in sensory evidence encoding that emerge with extended task exposure. This supports models implicating drift biases (in addition to starting point biases) in prior-informed decisions, with these drift biases potentially originating at the sensory level. The late emergence may explain why previous studies with fewer trials did not detect such effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C8, C76, C96-C98 represent the main interpretive conclusions. While the empirical findings (sensory modulation emerging late) are well-supported, the mechanistic interpretations are more speculative. C96 is explicitly speculative about why performance stabilized. C97-C98 tentatively link findings to drift bias models but acknowledge this requires formal modeling (not performed). C76's suggestion that previous studies missed effects due to fewer trials is plausible but not directly tested. These conclusions are reasonable inferences but go beyond what the data definitively demonstrate.

results.result: The manuscript situates the current work within an extensive literature on expectation effects in perceptual decision-making, reviewing evidence for both strategic criterion adjustments (starting point biases) and sensory-level modulations. The review covers computational models, neurophysiological findings across species, methodological challenges in dissociating expectation from attention, and theoretical frameworks including predictive coding and sharpening accounts.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3, C9-C23, C71-C72, C77-C86, C91-C93, C99-C107 provide a comprehensive literature review with extensive citations. These claims accurately represent the state of the field, including debates about whether expectations affect sensory processing and methodological challenges in cueing paradigms. The citations appear appropriate and the characterizations of prior work are balanced, noting both positive findings and mixed evidence. This contextualizes the current study's contributions effectively.

results.result: Participants exhibited typical behavioral biases in response to prior probability cues, with faster and more accurate responses on valid cue trials and slower, less accurate responses on invalid cue trials. These effects were stable across task exposure, with no significant interaction between cue validity and task exposure for either reaction time or accuracy.
results.evaluation: All reviewers acknowledged these behavioral findings without critique. The editor noted 'sophisticated analyses of human EEG data provide convincing evidence that both motor preparation and sensory processing were affected by expectations,' and Reviewer 2 stated the results 'convincingly demonstrate that both features of perceptual decision making are modulated by prior expectations.' The behavioral effects are treated as established and uncontroversial.

results.result: The SSVEP tracked differential contrast representing sensory evidence, with target gratings eliciting significantly greater SSVEP amplitude than non-target gratings. The marginal SSVEP significantly predicted both choice accuracy (positively) and reaction time (negatively), confirming it as a reliable neural index of encoded contrast evidence.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted the SSVEP as a valid measure of sensory encoding. Reviewer 2 praised the 'carefully-constructed experiment design' that 'allows separation of multiple electroencephalographic (EEG) signals' and noted the SSVEP 'can be cleanly dissociated from more anterior beta-band activity over motor cortex.' Reviewer 3 commended the 'clever use of the encephalogram (EEG)' and 'deft design choices' that 'allowed the authors to extract both contrast-dependent sensory signals and motor preparation signals.'

results.result: Cues evoked substantial biases in motor preparation (Mu-Beta lateralization) consistent with criterion adjustments, with significantly greater lateralization for cued compared to neutral trials. These motor preparation effects were present from the earliest trials and remained stable across task exposure.
results.evaluation: Reviewers uniformly accepted the motor preparation findings. The editor noted 'motor preparation...were affected by expectations,' Reviewer 2 stated the study 'allow[s] evaluation of how cued expectancy effects may unfold,' and Reviewer 3 noted 'expectation effects are immediately manifest in motor preparation signals.' No reviewer questioned the validity or interpretation of the motor preparation results.

results.result: Predictive cues produced significant modulation of the SSVEP during evidence presentation, with reduced marginal SSVEP following invalid cues compared to valid or neutral cues. Critically, this sensory-level effect only emerged with extended task exposure (circa 4 hours), showing a significant interaction between cue validity and task exposure, while motor preparation adjustments were present from the earliest trials.
results.evaluation: Reviewers raised substantial concerns about the SSVEP findings. Reviewer 1 noted 'a substantial portion of response times are earlier than all, or a portion of, the time period included in the SSVEP measurement window,' questioning whether 'contrast-dependent visual responses...indexed visual input that was actually used to make the decision.' They also stated 'there is no strong evidence for clear SSVEP modulations in any specific time windows leading to the response' and noted 'uncertainty regarding how to interpret the SSVEP effects.' While reviewers acknowledged the finding, they expressed doubt about its interpretation and relevance to decision-making.

results.result: The cues did not produce significant anticipatory modulation of sensory encoding during the baseline period before stimulus onset.
results.evaluation: This null finding was not challenged by reviewers. Reviewer 3 noted that 'expectation effects are immediately manifest in motor preparation signals and only emerge in sensory signals after extensive training,' implicitly accepting the absence of anticipatory sensory effects. The authors' discussion of why anticipatory effects were not observed (citing methodological differences from prior studies) was not contested.

results.result: SSVEP amplitudes were significantly larger for target compared to non-target gratings, but there was no significant interaction between cue condition and target/non-target status.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 specifically highlighted this as a limitation, stating 'there is some uncertainty regarding how to interpret the SSVEP effects' because 'the observed increase in marginal SSVEPs for validly as compared to invalidly cued trials could arise due to an increase in SSVEP amplitudes for target grating orientations, a decrease for non-target orientations, a combination of these two, or even an increase or decrease for both.' They noted 'some analyses were performed...but these did not provide clear evidence that favoured a specific interpretation.'

results.result: The difference between pre-response and post-response SSVEP increased with task exposure, but there was no main effect of cue validity and no interaction between cue validity and task exposure on this measure. Bayesian analyses provided no compelling evidence for cue effects post-response.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these post-response analyses. Reviewer 1's concerns focused on the pre-response period and the timing of SSVEP measurement relative to responses, but they did not dispute the post-response findings themselves.

results.result: There was significantly greater alpha desynchronization (indicating enhanced attention) in the neutral cue condition compared to cued conditions during the pre-evidence period.
results.evaluation: Reviewers positively received this finding. Reviewer 2 noted 'another interesting observation...is that neural signatures of focused attention are exaggerated on trials where participants are given neutral (i.e. uninformative) cues. This is consistent with the idea that observers are more attentive to incoming sensory evidence when they cannot rely on their expectations.' Reviewer 3 stated 'this hypothesis is consistent with the authors' thoughtful analysis showing decreased neural signatures of attention over posterior electrodes following predictive cues.'

results.result: The results suggest that probabilistic information can induce subtle biases in the encoding of sensory evidence itself, in addition to strategic adjustments to the decision process. These sensory-level effects emerged only with extensive task exposure, potentially allowing participants to stabilize performance despite reductions in available physical evidence. The findings tentatively support drift bias models in addition to starting point bias.
results.evaluation: Reviewers expressed mixed views on this central conclusion. Reviewer 1 stated 'an argument is made for changes in the evidence accumulation rate (called the drift rate)...however, this inference is limited by the fact that evidence accumulation models...were not used to test for drift rate changes' and noted 'plots of response quantiles...do not show a typical pattern that indicates changes in the drift rate.' Reviewer 2 acknowledged the study 'makes a strong contribution' but noted 'the paradigm...blurs together the processes of deciding about the stimulus and choosing/initiating the response,' limiting insights. The interpretation remains contested despite the data being acknowledged.

results.result: Marginal contrast was significantly reduced as a function of task exposure due to difficulty titration, but participant accuracy scores remained stable across task exposure.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these findings about task difficulty and performance stability. The stability of performance despite reduced contrast was used by the authors to support their interpretation about sensory modulation compensating for reduced evidence, though reviewers questioned that interpretation rather than the underlying data.

results.result: The study acknowledges methodological challenges in dissociating expectation from attention in cueing paradigms, as cues provide both probabilistic information and information about feature relevance. Feature-based attention has been shown to induce sensory modulations similar to those attributed to expectations.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly endorsed this concern. Reviewer 2 stated 'the principal shortcoming of this study is that the experimental task confounds expectations about stimulus identity with expectations about to-be-performed responses' and noted the paradigm 'blurs together the processes of deciding about the stimulus and choosing/initiating the response.' Reviewer 3 suggested 'one interesting possibility is that perceptual expectations are not automatic but demand the deployment of feature-based attention.' The authors' acknowledgment of these limitations was viewed positively.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on behavioral findings (C24-C40). Both OpenEval and peer reviewers found the statistical evidence for cue validity effects on RT and accuracy to be convincing and well-supported. No concerns were raised by either evaluation.

Perfect agreement on SSVEP validity (C43-C47, C73-C74). Both evaluations accepted that SSVEP tracks contrast and predicts behavior, with peer reviewers praising the experimental design that allows clean separation of EEG signals.

Perfect agreement on post-response analyses (C62-C66). Both evaluations accepted the null findings regarding post-decisional confirmation bias. OpenEval noted appropriate use of both frequentist and Bayesian analyses; peer reviewers did not challenge these findings.

Agreement on motor preparation findings (C4, C55-C57). Both evaluations found the motor beta lateralization results well-supported. OpenEval emphasized the lack of task exposure effects; peer reviewers uniformly accepted that motor preparation was affected by expectations without critique.

Agreement on absence of anticipatory sensory effects (C48). Both evaluations accepted this null finding. OpenEval noted it was appropriately reported; peer reviewers implicitly accepted it without challenge.

Agreement on alpha oscillation findings (C67-C70, C87-C90). Both evaluations found evidence for differential engagement across cue conditions convincing. Peer reviewers positively received the finding and noted consistency with attention deployment when expectations are unavailable.

Agreement on task difficulty manipulation (C41-C42). Both evaluations accepted the findings about contrast reduction and performance stability. OpenEval noted relevance for interpreting sensory modulation emergence; peer reviewers did not challenge the underlying data.

Disagreement on mechanistic interpretations (C5, C8, C76, C96-C98). OpenEval rated these claims as UNCERTAIN, noting they are speculative and go beyond what data demonstrate. Peer reviewers also rated UNCERTAIN but were more critical, specifically noting lack of formal drift diffusion modeling and questioning the drift rate interpretation based on response quantile plots.

Significant disagreement on SSVEP temporal dynamics during evidence presentation (C7, C58-C61, C94). OpenEval found the evidence SUPPORTED with robust statistical models showing cue×task exposure interaction. Peer reviewers rated UNCERTAIN, raising substantial concerns about timing of SSVEP measurement relative to responses and questioning whether measured signals actually indexed evidence used for decisions.

Disagreement on interpretation of cue effects on SSVEP (C53-C54). OpenEval found the pattern of invalid cue suppression well-documented and SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers rated UNCERTAIN, specifically noting inability to determine whether effects arose from target enhancement, non-target suppression, or combinations thereof.

Partial overlap on sensory modulation claims (C49-C52, C75). OpenEval found clear evidence SUPPORTED that cues modulate sensory encoding during evidence presentation. Peer reviewers rated overlapping claims (including these) as UNCERTAIN due to concerns about SSVEP measurement timing and interpretation of what signals represent.

Agreement on methodological limitations (C99-C102). OpenEval rated the literature review and contextualization as SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers explicitly endorsed the authors' acknowledgment of confounding between stimulus expectations and response expectations, viewing this transparency positively.

OpenEval evaluated sample characteristics and frequency bias issues (C108-C111, C116-C120) as SUPPORTED, commending transparency while noting small sample size limits generalizability. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addressed these methodological details.
